nodes.question: What impact have ECAs had on fossil fuel investments in recipient countries?
nodes.answer: ECAs have contributed billions of dollars in public finance for fossil fuels, which has helped to lock-in recipient countries to fossil fuel energy systems.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Achieving a clean energy transition requires global financial flows to be redirected away from fossil fuels and into renewable energy. While capital market actors and multilateral financial institutions have been the subject of significant scholarly attention, public bilat - eral financial institutions, especially Export Credit Agencies (ECAs), have been largely overlooked. This is an important oversight given ECAs are the source of billions of dollars of public finance for fossil fuels, which has helped to lock-in recipient countries to fossil fuel energy systems. Using a panel dataset of ECA transactions in the energy sector, we show that despite some improvements in financial flows after the Paris Agreement in 2015, fossil fuel investments remain pervasive and growth in clean energy investments is mini - mal. To better understand changes in ECA portfolios, we examine the cases of the Export- Import Bank of the United States (Exlm) and UK Export Finance (UKEF). Drawing on elite interviews, we identify three factors that are shaping Exlm S and UKEF S capacity to promote renewable energy exports: the extent of political control over the bureaucracy, the size and composition of green industrial bases, and the policy tools available to both ECAs to support the renewables sector.

nodes.question: How do ECAs have the potential to align with national climate policy objectives?
nodes.answer: As institutions controlled by national governments, ECAs can leverage their financial instruments to encourage private investment in clean energy projects.
nodes.paragraph: 2018 ). While capital market actors and multilateral financial institutions have been the subject of significant scholarly attention (Kim and Lee 2021 ; Stoll et al. 2021 ; Ameli et al. 2020 ), public bilateral financial institutions, especially Export Credit Agencies (ECAs), have been largely overlooked (Peterson and Downie 2023 ; Klasen et al. 2022 This is an important oversight given that ECAs are the largest source of bilateral public finance for fossil fuels, which has helped to lock-in recipient countries to fossil fuel energy systems, such as coal fired power stations in Asia and gas infrastructure in Africa (O Manique et al. 2024 ; Chen et al. 2021 ). At the same time, as institutions under the control of national governments, ECAs, unlike private capital or multilateral financial institutions, should be well placed to respond to national climate policy objectives, and use their financial instruments, such as risk insur - ance, to crowd-in private investment for clean energy projects. In this context, it is no surprise that ECAs are facing growing international pressure to align their activities with the goals of the Paris Agreement.

nodes.question: What coalition was launched by European countries in 2021, and what was its purpose?
nodes.answer: The Export Finance for Future (E3F) coalition was launched to align export finance with international climate objectives.
nodes.paragraph: For example, in 2015 OECD countries agreed to restrict export finance for coal-fired power projects (Liao 2021 ). In 2021 European countries launched the Export Finance for Future (E3F) coalition to specifically align export finance with international climate objectives (E3F 2023 ). In the same year, 34 countries signed the Glasgow Statement, which commits signatories to ending public financial support for international fossil fuel projects (DuFour et al. 2022 ). At the national level, many G20 governments have responded by implementing new climate targets. For example, in 2022 European ECAs committed to ending export credit for fossil fuel energy projects (IISD 2022 ), and several other ECAs, including the Export-Import Bank of the US (Exlm) and the UK Export Finance (UKEF) have announced policies to limit public finance for fossil fuels (DuFour et al. 2022 ). While the pressure on ECAs is likely to increase, we do not have a good understanding of the potential for these public bilateral financial institutions to accelerate a clean energy transition. Similarly, there is a lack of scholarly work on the capacity of ECAs as distinct financial institutions with unique organizational structures, competencies, resources, mandates, and institutional histories to effectively engage in clean energy finance. In this paper, we address these gaps in the literature. We first present descriptive statis - tics of ECA investments from 2005 2023 for select G20 countries. We show that despite some improvements in the post-Paris period, fossil fuel investments remain pervasive and growth in clean energy investments is minimal. For example, ECAs from China and Japan maintained in excess of $4 billion USD in average annual fossil fuel lending since 2015, while Canada and South Korea averaged over $2 billion USD in annual fossil fuel spending. nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What commitments have Exlm and UKEF made regarding their portfolios?
nodes.answer: Both ECAs have committed to greening their portfolios despite mandates to promote national exports, including fossil fuels.
nodes.paragraph: To better understand changes in ECA portfolios at the organizational level, we conduct two in-depth case studies of ECAs. To do so, we draw on elite interviews with Exlm and UKEF. Despite their mandates to promote national exports including fossil fuels, both ECAs are now governed by a suite of climate change policies and have made commitments to green their portfolios, with varying levels of success. We identify three key factors that affect the capacity of Exlm and UKEF to promote renewable exports. First, is the extent of political control of the bureaucracy, which directly affects how responsive ECAs are to pressure from the executive and legislatures to transi - tion their lending portfolios towards renewable energy. In the US, Exlm S statutory auton - omy has resulted in the bank resisting executive orders to limit fossil fuel lending. Whereas UKEF, which as a government department does not have statutory autonomy, has directly responded to executive pressure by transitioning its lending portfolio. Second is the size of the state S green industrial base. In countries with mature renewable energy industries, which have satisfied domestic demand, there will be more demand for export credits.

nodes.paragraph: 2021 ; Hughes and Downie 2021 ). Systematic analyses of ECA financial flows in the energy sector remain limited (Censkowsky et al. 2025 ). Similarly, there is a lack of scholarly work on the capacity of ECAs as distinct financial institutions with unique organizational structures, competencies, resources, mandates, and institutional histories to effectively engage in clean energy finance. In this paper, we address these gaps in the literature. We first present descriptive statis - tics of ECA investments from 2005 2023 for select G20 countries. We show that despite some improvements in the post-Paris period, fossil fuel investments remain pervasive and growth in clean energy investments is minimal. For example, ECAs from China and Japan maintained in excess of $4 billion USD in average annual fossil fuel lending since 2015, while Canada and South Korea averaged over $2 billion USD in annual fossil fuel spending. However, there have also been notable increases in clean energy spending amongst some 1340 Climatic Change (2025) 178:40 ECAs, particularly the United Kingdom, which grew its annual clean energy lending from a pre-Paris average of $8.7 million USD to $64 million USD in the post-Paris period.

nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What commitment have both Exlm and UKEF made regarding their portfolios?
nodes.answer: Both ECAs have made commitments to green their portfolios, although with varying levels of success.
nodes.paragraph: To better understand changes in ECA portfolios at the organizational level, we conduct two in-depth case studies of ECAs. To do so, we draw on elite interviews with Exlm and UKEF. Despite their mandates to promote national exports including fossil fuels, both ECAs are now governed by a suite of climate change policies and have made commitments to green their portfolios, with varying levels of success. We identify three key factors that affect the capacity of Exlm and UKEF to promote renewable exports. First, is the extent of political control of the bureaucracy, which directly affects how responsive ECAs are to pressure from the executive and legislatures to transi - tion their lending portfolios towards renewable energy. In the US, Exlm S statutory auton - omy has resulted in the bank resisting executive orders to limit fossil fuel lending. Whereas UKEF, which as a government department does not have statutory autonomy, has directly responded to executive pressure by transitioning its lending portfolio. Second is the size of the state S green industrial base. In countries with mature renewable energy industries, which have satisfied domestic demand, there will be more demand for export credits.
